2.1 complaint data and other zip-code or county-level data


Data on consumer complaints come from the CFPB’s website. Hayes,
Jiang, and Pan [2021] provide a detailed description of this database. For
our analysis, we use complaint data from two sample periods. Our COVID
sample period is from August 2019 to September 2020, which centers
around the national emergency declaration in March 2020. This sample
consists of complaints filed from 50 states and the District of Columbia,
and we require that the consumer’s location information, either the 3-digit
(first three digits) or 5-digit zip code, is available. We construct balanced
samples both at the 3-digit and 5-digit zip-code level (see the appendix for
details) and report the summary statistics in panel A of table 1 and panel

2.2 data on csr and corporate leadership


We obtain CSR data from MSCI ESG KLD STATS, which rates over 2,400
companies in the MSCI USA Investable Marketable Index along seven
ESG dimensions: environmental performance, community activities, human rights, employee relations, diversity, product quality, and governance. <sup>5</sup>

In each dimension, companies receive ratings (zero or one) for a number
of “strengths” and “concerns.” We create an overall score for each dimension by subtracting its concern score from its strength score (see appendix
for details) and add the overall scores across the seven dimensions to get
_Overall ESG_, measured in 2018.

In addition to aggregate ESG performance, we study two of the dimensions that are most pertinent to our study: product quality and diversity. The
product dimension is most likely to be relevant to consumer complaints.
_Product_, which includes ratings regarding product quality and consumer
relationships, is the score for this dimension. Because we focus on the financial services industry, we also examine a subcategory under the product
dimension, _Transparent lending_ . This rating assesses how companies manage
the risks associated with unanticipated credit losses, litigation, and regulatory changes brought by offering financial products that lack transparency
or are likely to be financially unsustainable to the end user. Companies that
offer transparent financial products based on a borrower’s ability to repay
score higher (i.e., one) on this dimension.

We also seek to understand the role of inclusive corporate culture in reducing the racial gap in financial complaints, using the diversity dimension
( _Diversity_ is the score for this dimension). <sup>6</sup> The strengths in this dimension measure diversity in a firm’s management, board, and workforce. The
concerns measure controversies due to discrimination-related legal cases
or criticisms. While most of the subcategories in this dimension focus on

rates whether the company has made notable progress in the promotion
of women and minorities, particularly to line positions with profit-and-loss
responsibilities in the corporation.

In addition to using the KLD data, we collect information about board
diversity for the publicly traded financial institutions in our sample, explained in detail in the appendix. Because a strong diversity culture likely
needs critical mass in leadership, we construct an indicator variable, _High_
_board_ _diversity_, which equals one if at least one-third of the firm’s directors
are reported as female or minorities. Under this definition, firms with high
board diversity are those whose male, non-minority directors do not constitute a supermajority on the board (where a supermajority vote is sometimes
required for crucial corporate decisions such as amending bylaws). About
60% of institutions in our COVID period sample have high board diversity
based on this definition. This indicator variable significantly correlates with
_Diversity_ at 0.29. We report summary statistics for these measures in panel E
and revisit them in section 4.3.

complaint data


Data on consumer complaints come from the CFPB’s website. During
the COVID sample period (August 2019 to September 2020), there are
375,420 complaints with available 3-digit zip-code information, and 188,731
complaints with available 5-digit zip-code information, as the CFPB may
mask the last two digits or all five digits of the zip code for privacy reasons.

We calculate the total number of complaints each month for a given
3-digit (or 5-digit) zip code and balance the panel whenever a zip code
has at least one complaint during the sample period. We then calculate _Per_
_capita complaints_, the number of complaints per 100,000 people in a 3-digit
(or 5-digit) zip code. The CFPB publishes the consumer’s 5-digit zip code,
except where the population in a zip code contains fewer than 20,000 people. In these cases, CFPB will publish either the first three digits of the zip
code or no zip code data, depending on the population of the consumer’s
area.

other zip code– or county-level data


We collect the 5-digit zip code–level demographic information from
the 2018 ACS and aggregate them to the 3-digit zip-code level using the
population-weighted average values. _Nonwhite_ is the fraction of the local
population that reported a race that is not “White alone.” Besides “White
alone,” the ACS race table includes “Black or African American alone,”
which is the largest non-white group in this table, “American Indian and
Alaska Native alone,” “Asian alone,” “Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific
Islander alone,” “Some Other Race alone,” and “Two or More Races.” “Hispanic” is not defined by census as a race, but as an ethnicity. Therefore,
people of Hispanic or Latino origin can select various different races in
this table, and many offer write-in responses. <sup>30</sup>

We use the fraction of residents in the zip code–county link file provided by
the Office of Policy Development and Research to allocate the COVID-19
cases to each zip code in a given county. <sup>32</sup>

data on csr and corporate leadership

We obtain CSR data from MSCI ESG KLD STATS, which compiles information from company disclosures (10-Ks, sustainability reports, proxy
statements, etc.), as well as academic, government, and NGO datasets in
order to rate companies along ESG dimensions that include environment
performance, community activities, human rights, employee relations, diversity, product quality, and governance. <sup>35</sup> In each dimension, companies
receive ratings (zero or one) for a number of “strengths” (positive ESG
policies or practices) and “concerns” (negative ESG policies). For each financial institution in our sample that is rated by MSCI in 2018 (the latest
year with available ESG data), we calculate the average strength and average
concern in each dimension, across all subcategories under that dimension
(see, e.g., Lins, Servaes, and Tamayo [2017]). Since the maximum number of strengths and concerns for any given dimension varies over time, we
scale each firm-year’s strength (concern) scores for each dimension by the
maximum number of strengths (concerns) possible for that dimension in
that year. Therefore, the strength and concern scores for each dimension
range from zero to one. We then create an overall score for each dimension by subtracting its concern score from its strength score, and we add
the overall scores across the seven dimensions to get _Overall ESG_ .
